jobs.title: Research Fellow – Transition to Independence Programme in Cancer and Genomic Medicine
jobs.description:
The **Italian Institute for Genomic Medicine (IIGM)** is a leading research center dedicated to advancing precision medicine through cutting-edge genomics, bioinformatics, and translational research. Located in **Turin**, it brings together an international team of scientists and clinicians working at the interface of basic biology and clinical applications, with strong collaborations across academia, hospitals, and industry. With state-of-the-art facilities and a dynamic, multidisciplinary environment, IIGM offers an inspiring setting for innovation aimed at improving human health.

**Gender Equality Plan**: diversity is our legacy and our future. Be part of it. At **IIGM** diversity is an integral part of our culture and identity and for this we have adopted a plan for gender equality (GEP). We promote diversity and inclusion because we recognize that they are a source of strength and competitive advantage.

  
  

**Posizione:**
--------------

**The Italian Institute for Genomic Medicine (IIGM)** invites applications to its Transition to Independence Programme, designed for outstanding researchers who are ready to establish a recognizable independent scientific profile and prepare for the next step of professional growth.

**IIGM is entering a new phase of scientific expansion, with investment in new research programmes, recruitment, core facilities and enabling technologies.** The Programme is intended to give talented early-career scientists the protected space, resources and visibility needed to develop an autonomous research direction while remaining embedded in a highly collaborative cancer and genomic medicine environment.

**Research environment**

IIGM is based at the Candiolo Cancer Institute (INOC) near Turin and operates in close interaction with clinical, translational and basic research groups. The Institute combines expertise in cancer biology, genomics, epigenetics, computational biology and precision oncology, with access to shared technological platforms and a strong culture of interdisciplinary collaboration. The current expansion phase is creating new opportunities for scientific cross-fertilization, access to advanced technologies, and the development of emerging independent research lines.

**Requisiti:**
--------------

**Who should apply**

We are seeking advanced postdoctoral or equivalent researchers with a strong scientific record and clear potential for independence. Competitive applicants should demonstrate:

**About STEP-UP:**

STEP-UP is a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Network investigating pedestrian behavior and mobility in urban environments. Its research focuses on three areas: individual and interpersonal aspects of pedestrian behavior, environmental and infrastructural barriers to walking, and interactions between pedestrians and other road users. The aim is to improve the understanding of pedestrian mobility and support the development of safer and more inclusive urban public spaces.

STEP-UP brings together academic and non-academic partners to train 10 PhD students through an international Joint Doctorate program. The candidates benefit from joint supervision by researchers at partner institutions, an integrated doctoral training program, and opportunities for interdisciplinary and cross-sectoral collaboration, including research secondments at partner organizations. In addition to specialized scientific knowledge, they develop transferable skills in areas such as research communication and dissemination. The program prepares them for careers in research and other fields related to transport and urban development.

**About the Individual Research Project (IRP 5):**

Road lighting plays a crucial role in how road infrastructure and its surroundings are perceived at night. Effective road lighting design must consider not only objective visibility conditions but also their subjective evaluation. Adequate lighting should enhance both the actual visibility and the subjective sense of safety. However, current research reveals significant gaps in our understanding – both in defining the psychological components of perceived safety and in identifying the critical lighting conditions that influence it. The objective of this IRP is to investigate the defining criteria of perceived safety and its relationship to objective visibility conditions resulting from road lighting characteristics. The project will consider both aspects across diverse demographic groups (e.g., young adults, women, and the elderly) in comparison to middle-aged male pedestrians, and under various lighting scenarios. To achieve this, the research is structured around three sub-objectives: (1) Design and conduct studies to gather subjective data on perceived safety, including focus group interviews and on-site surveys combined with lighting measurements; (2) Develop and implement VR or screen-based experiments, systematically varying objective lighting conditions in controlled environments to collect related subjective responses; (3) Identify and quantify the key factors influencing pedestrians’ perceived safety at night, using methods such as clustering, data integration, and modelling, and drawing on expertise from both lighting engineering and traffic psychology.

This IRP is co-supervised by Lund University (Sweden). The PhD student will be enrolled both at TUD and Lund University, and will receive two PhD degrees upon completion of the program. The IRP includes a 12-month secondment to Lund to conduct an observational study.

**Your responsibilities**
-------------------------

Duties primarily include teaching and research. Research associates may also pursue further academic qualifications outside of their work responsibilities.

We invite applications for a research associate position in the research group Dynamics of Correlated Quantum Matter within the Cluster of Excellence CUI. Our research aims to understand how quantum materials can be controlled and transformed using nonequilibrium protocols, and how transient or metastable states of matter can be created on ultrafast timescales.

A central part of our work is the development of new theoretical and computational tools for the microscopic simulation of strongly interacting quantum systems far from equilibrium. In particular, we develop and apply nonequilibrium Green’s-function techniques and extensions of nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), combined with tensor-network approaches and machine-learning techniques.

The Research Associate will contribute to advancing these methods and applying them to fundamental questions in nonequilibrium quantum matter. Possible research directions include:

* Time-resolved spectroscopy of quantum materials: Developing a microscopic theoretical description of time-resolved spectroscopies in solids, with a particular focus on ultrafast X-ray spectroscopies and their ability to probe transient many-body states.

* Ultrafast phase transitions and metastability: Understanding microscopic pathways toward photoinduced and ultrafast phase transitions, including the interplay between electronic and lattice degrees of freedom, ultrafast disordering processes, and the formation and lifetime of metastable states.

* Current-driven quantum matter: Exploring unconventional states and phase transitions induced by intense electrical currents, and identifying new regimes of strongly driven correlated systems beyond conventional near-equilibrium descriptions.

Depending on the background and interests of the successful candidate, the project can place greater emphasis on the development of new computational and theoretical methods or on the microscopic modeling and understanding of nonequilibrium phenomena in quantum materials. We particularly welcome applicants who are interested in connecting methodological advances with experimentally relevant questions in ultrafast and nonequilibrium quantum matter.

The position offers the opportunity to work at the interface of strongly correlated quantum systems, nonequilibrium many-body theory, ultrafast spectroscopy, tensor-network methods, and machine learning, within the collaborative research environment of the Cluster of Excellence “CUI: Advanced Imaging of Matter”.
